nameStory: This grasshopper earned its name from two standout features: its notably short wings that don't fully cover its body, and the bright green coloration of the males. The 'short-winged' part is especially fitting since these wings are so stubby they look almost comically undersized compared to other grasshoppers!
description: The Short-winged Green Grasshopper is a small, compact member of the slant-faced grasshopper family found throughout New England. Males are typically bright green with a distinctively angled face that slopes backward, while females are usually brown and noticeably larger than their male counterparts. These grasshoppers are on the smaller side compared to many of their relatives, making them easy to overlook in grassy areas where they spend most of their time.

idTips.label: Slanted Face
idTips.description: The face angles backward dramatically from bottom to top, creating a distinctive wedge-shaped profile when viewed from the side

idTips.label: Short Wings
idTips.description: Wings are stubby and don't reach the end of the abdomen, feeling almost leathery to the touch rather than thin and papery

idTips.label: Male Coloration
idTips.description: Males display a vibrant grass-green color that can seem almost artificial in bright sunlight

idTips.label: Female Appearance
idTips.description: Females are typically brown with a mottled pattern and are noticeably bulkier and longer than males

idTips.label: Size Difference
idTips.description: The size difference between males and females is striking - females can appear almost twice as large

idTips.label: Body Feel
idTips.description: When gently handled, they feel surprisingly solid and chunky for their size, with a smooth, almost waxy texture

habitat: Short-winged Green Grasshoppers thrive in open grassy areas including meadows, field edges, roadsides, and suburban lawns throughout New England. They prefer areas with mixed grasses and low-growing plants, often found in slightly disturbed habitats rather than pristine wilderness. Look for them in sunny spots where the grass isn't too dense, from sea level up to moderate elevations in the region.

seasonality.spring: Adults are not yet active; eggs are overwintering in soil and will begin hatching as temperatures warm in late spring.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when both males and females are most visible and active, with bright green males easiest to spot in early to mid-summer.
seasonality.fall: Adults remain active into early fall, with mating and egg-laying occurring before the first hard frosts end their season.
seasonality.winter: No visible activity above ground; eggs remain dormant in soil until spring warming triggers hatching.

funFact: The males are such bright green that they can actually look fake or toy-like in person - many people's first reaction is to wonder if someone dropped a plastic grasshopper in the grass!
confusionNotes: The dramatic sexual dimorphism means males and females are often mistaken for completely different species - remember that the tiny bright green ones and the larger brown ones are actually the same species! The slanted face is your best clue that they're related.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'short-horned' grasshoppers, the 'horns' actually refer to their antennae, not any horn-like structures on their heads - this family name distinguishes them from long-horned grasshoppers (katydids) which have much longer, thread-like antennae.
compareHints: Since this is the only Dichromorpha species in New England, compare it to other small slant-faced grasshoppers in the area. The combination of extremely short wings and the dramatic color difference between males and females sets it apart from most other local grasshopper species. The bright green males are particularly distinctive among New England's slant-faced grasshopper community.
